Evasion
ē-vā´zhŭn
n. (a shift or excuse by which a duty or a truth is escaped)
Latin evasio, from evadere, to go out, escape. An evasion does not deny the claim; it goes round it.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

An evasion is an escape from a duty by a device that keeps the appearance of obedience. The Lord names one by its technical term: “ye say, If a man shall say to his father or mother, It is Corban, that is to say, a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me; he shall be free… making the word of God of none effect through your tradition” (Mar 7:11–13). Adam evades in the garden — “The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat” (Gen 3:12) — and Cain after him: “Am I my brother's keeper?” (Gen 4:9). The excuses of the invited are gathered in one parable: “they all with one consent began to make excuse” (Luk 14:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines evasion as the act of eluding or avoiding, particularly the pressure of an argument, accusation, charge, or interrogatory; artifice to elude; shift; equivocation; subterfuge.

EVASION, n. The act of eluding or avoiding, particularly the pressure of an argument, accusation, charge or interrogatory; artifice to elude; shift; equivocation; excuse; subterfuge.

Key Scripture

Mar 7:11 — "But ye say, If a man shall say to his father or mother, It is Corban, that is to say, a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me; he shall be free."

Mar 7:13 — "Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered: and many such like things do ye."

Gen 3:12 — "And the man said, The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat."

Gen 4:9 — "And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?"

Luk 14:18 — "And they all with one consent began to make excuse. The first said unto him, I have bought a piece of ground, and I must needs go and see it: I pray thee have me excused."

Modern Corruption

A duty is escaped by a device that looks more pious than the duty, and Corban was a religious word used to avoid feeding a parent.

expand to see more

Mark 7 is the classic case and its cleverness is the point. The fifth commandment requires a man to support his father and mother; the evasion was to declare the money Corban — devoted to God — after which he was, by the tradition, released from the obligation, and there is no indication the money had to leave his hands. The device was not irreligious; it was more religious than the duty it displaced, and that is what made it work. The Lord's verdict is the most severe thing He says about tradition: making the word of God of none effect. An evasion of this kind always finds a higher-sounding principle to shelter under.

The first two evasions in Scripture set the pattern for all of them, and neither is a lie. Adam's statement is entirely true — the woman did give him the fruit, and God did give him the woman — and it is an evasion because it answers a question that was not asked; God asked hast thou eaten, and got a history of how it came about. Cain's is a counter-question, which is the second-oldest technique. Neither man denies the fact. Both relocate the subject, and every human conversation about guilt since has used one of the two.

Luke 14:18 shows the polite form, which is the one most of us use: they all with one consent began to make excuse, and the excuses are reasonable — a field bought, oxen to prove, a wife married. Nothing in the list is sinful in itself. That is the difficulty with evasion as a category: it is almost never made out of bad things, and the man doing it can usually produce a defensible reason. The test is simply whether the thing required got done.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek korban (G2878), a gift devoted to God; paraiteomai (G3868), to beg off, make excuse; prophasis (G4392), a pretext; Hebrew ma'aneh, an answer turned aside.

expand to see more

Greek korban (G2878) — a gift, that is, devoted; Mark 7:11 only, with Matthew 15:5.

Greek paraiteomai (G3868) — to make excuse, beg off; Luke 14:18–19, Hebrews 12:19, 12:25.

Greek prophasis (G4392) — pretext, cloke; John 15:22, 1 Thessalonians 2:5.

Usage

"“It is Corban… he shall be free” — a device more religious than the duty it displaced."

"“The woman whom thou gavest to be with me” — entirely true, and not the answer to the question."

"“They all with one consent began to make excuse” — and nothing on the list was sinful."
